title: Why a Billion-Dollar Company Can Run Out of Cash
central_question: How can a business look wealthy and profitable yet fail to pay a bill that is due today?
fiction_notice: Marigold and her company are fictional. Figures are illustrative and internally consistent, not taken from any real business.

financials.note: cash_paid_out = expenses paid in cash (1,900,000) + extra stock bought for next quarter (300,000). Stock is an asset until sold, so it reduces cash but not profit.

scenes.narration: Meet Marigold. Her company is worth millions on paper. So why can't it pay one bill that's due today?
scenes.caption: Worth millions. Can't pay one bill.

scenes.narration: Customers are buying everything. Sales are up, orders are stacking up, and the profit report says: best year ever.
scenes.caption: Sales up. Orders up. Profit up.

scenes.narration: Here's the catch. Sell on credit, and the sale counts straight away. The actual cash arrives later. Sometimes months later.
scenes.caption: Sale recorded today. Cash arrives later.

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, money going out won't wait. Wages are due Friday. Suppliers want paying on delivery. Stock is bought before it's sold.
scenes.caption: Wages. Suppliers. Stock. Paid now.

scenes.narration: Picture a reservoir of cash you can spend today, and a long pipeline of money customers still owe you. Today's bill waits at a gate that only takes cash.
scenes.caption: Cash you have now is not the same as money you are owed.

scenes.narration: More invoices land. A supplier pauses deliveries. The profit report says five hundred thousand. The bank says forty.
scenes.caption: Profit: $500k. Cash: $40k. Bill due: $120k.

scenes.narration: Profit measures what a business earned over a period. Cash flow tracks money actually moving in and out. When the timing slips, even a profitable business can hit trouble. It's not the only way companies fail, but Australian liquidators name cash-flow problems more than any other single cause.
scenes.caption: Profit = earned over a period. Cash flow = money moving in and out.
scenes.subcaption: ASIC 2022-23: cash-flow problems cited in 52% of liquidator reports

scenes.narration: Then: ping. A big customer finally pays. The reservoir fills, the supplier's back, and Marigold celebrates. Briefly.
scenes.caption: A big customer finally pays: $350,000

scenes.narration: Lesson learned: being rich on paper is lovely. Paying people in actual money is even better.
scenes.caption: Rich on paper is lovely. Paying people in actual money is better.
scenes.subcaption: THE HIDDEN WORLD. Everything has a secret.

claims.text: Under accrual accounting, a credit sale is recorded as income when it is earned/invoiced, even though the cash is received later.

Profit measures what a business earned over a period; cash flow tracks the actual movement of cash in and out. A statement of cash flows exists precisely because profit alone does not show an entity's ability to generate cash and meet obligations.

Businesses need cash to pay suppliers and employees on time (operating cash outflows), and a profitable business can run into trouble if cash inflows and outflows are mistimed. This is one mechanism of failure, not the only one.
In ASIC's 2022-23 insolvency statistics, 'inadequate cash flow or high cash use' was the most frequently nominated cause of company failure, cited in 52% of registered liquidators' reports.
Marigold's company and all its figures are fictional and internally consistent: revenue 2.4M, expenses 1.9M, profit 0.5M, receivables 0.6M, cash 40k, bill due 120k.
Reservoir (cash available now) versus pipeline (receivables still flowing in) is a visual metaphor, not an accounting definition.
